name: Java
scope: A person with INTERMEDIATE proficiency level in Java as a competency should be able to / is capable of writing and debugging production-ready applications using core Java constructs (loops, conditionals, generics, annotations, Collections Framework) while applying OOP principles (inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, abstraction). They demonstrate moderate concurrency skills (Threads, Runnables, Executors) with a basic grasp of the Java Memory Model, follow SOLID principles to avoid code smells, and effectively use frameworks like Spring (Spring Boot, MVC, Data) or Jakarta EE for building web applications, REST APIs, and microservices, integrating common logging (SLF4J, Log4j) and security (Spring Security). They employ ORM libraries (JPA/Hibernate) to map entities to relational databases (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle) with an understanding of eager vs. lazy loading and manage environment-based configurations using build tools like Maven and Gradle. They containerize applications with Docker, have some exposure to cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure), and set up CI/CD pipelines (Jenkins, GitLab CI, GitHub Actions) for automated builds, tests, and deployments. They write unit and integration tests (JUnit, TestNG) with mocking (Mockito), measure coverage with Jacoco or SonarQube, and practice basic TDD or BDD if required. They troubleshoot performance issues using profiling tools (VisualVM, JDK Mission Control, YourKit), refine inefficient queries, and optimize concurrency and data structures. They address fundamental security concerns (parameterized queries, handling secrets), apply microservices concepts (service discovery, circuit breakers), and incorporate resilience patterns. They also adopt relevant design patterns (Singleton, Factory, Strategy, Observer), use diagramming tools (UML, PlantUML) for architecture visualization, and collaborate through code reviews and documentation (Confluence, GitHub Wiki). Overall, they consistently deliver maintainable, high-quality Java solutions suitable for enterprise projects, while guiding junior developers on best practices and ensuring solid team communication.
long_scope:
Below is an exhaustive view of the scope for an INTERMEDIATE Java professional—generally someone with around 3–5 years of experience. This scope covers what such an engineer should be able to accomplish, the tasks they commonly handle, the outcomes they should deliver, the tools they typically use, and the concepts and frameworks they have gained mastery over. While not as broadly experienced or deeply specialized as an ADVANCED (6–10+ years) or EXPERT (10++ years) professional, an INTERMEDIATE practitioner goes beyond fundamental syntax and small-scale coding, consistently applying core Java skills to deliver production-ready solutions.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. LANGUAGE FUNDAMENTALS & CODE QUALITY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Solid Grasp of Java Syntax and Core Concepts  
  – Comfortable using loops, conditionals, and core language features (e.g., generics, annotations).  
  – Understands polymorphism, inheritance, encapsulation, and abstraction in practice (not just theory).  
• Consistent Application of Best Practices  
  – Writes modular, maintainable, and legible code without major code smells.  
  – Employs naming conventions, consistent formatting, and follows style guidelines (e.g., Google Java Style or company-specific guidelines).  
• Basic to Intermediate Knowledge of Java Memory Model  
  – Understands how objects are allocated, the difference between heap and stack, and the basics of garbage collection.  
  – Can troubleshoot common memory issues (e.g., OutOfMemoryError) through profiling and basic heap analysis.  

Outcome/Tasks:  
– Produces code that is readable, maintainable, performs well enough for typical business use cases.  
– Uses language constructs appropriately to reduce bugs and confusion, ensuring reliable day-to-day functionality.  

Tools:  
– Common IDEs (Eclipse, IntelliJ IDEA, VS Code with Java extensions).  
– Style/quality plugins (Checkstyle, SonarLint, PMD).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. CORE LIBRARIES, APIs, & UTILITIES
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Collections & Generics  
  – Uses the Java Collections Framework (List, Set, Map) effectively, choosing the right collection for the task.  
  – Demonstrates comfort in advanced operations (sorting, searching, transformations) using built-in library methods.  
• Java Stream API  
  – Knows how to transform and filter collections using streams, lambda expressions, and method references.  
  – Handles potential performance implications of streams on large data sets.  
• Concurrency & Multithreading (Foundational Level)  
  – Utilizes basic concurrency constructs (Thread, Runnable, Callable, Future, Executors).  
  – Recognizes thread-safety concerns and can apply synchronization or locks to avoid data races.  
  – Familiar with using higher-level concurrency tools such as CompletableFuture for asynchronous workflows.  

Outcome/Tasks:  
– Implements data processing workflows leveraging Java collections and streams.  
– Creates simple concurrent or parallel routines that improve responsiveness or throughput.  

Tools:  
– Built-in concurrency utilities in java.util.concurrent.  
– Profilers that trace concurrency metrics (VisualVM, JMC).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. OBJECT-ORIENTED DESIGN & DESIGN PATTERNS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Application of Common Design Patterns  
  – Comfortable implementing patterns such as Singleton, Factory, Strategy, Observer, and Builder.  
  – Understands the trade-offs and scenarios where these patterns are most useful.  
• Code Reusability and Abstraction  
  – Identifies opportunities to abstract common functionality into reusable components.  
  – Demonstrates an understanding of SOLID principles (Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, Dependency Inversion).  

Outcome/Tasks:  
– Decomposes features into modules or classes aligned with accepted design principles.  
– Avoids overdesign by prioritizing maintainability and clarity.  

Tools:  
– UML diagramming tools (e.g., PlantUML, Lucidchart) for visualizing class relationships.  
– Architectural notes in Confluence or similar documentation platforms.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. FRAMEWORKS & ECOSYSTEM KNOWLEDGE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Comfort with Popular Java Frameworks  
  – Works confidently with Spring or Java EE (Jakarta EE) for building web applications, RESTful APIs, or microservices.  
  – Understands key modules in Spring, e.g., Spring Core, Spring MVC, Spring Boot, Spring Data, and basic security configurations.  
• Persistence & ORM  
  – Uses JPA/Hibernate or other ORM frameworks to map Java objects to relational databases.  
  – Knows how to define entities, relationships, and handle common performance considerations (lazy vs. eager loading).  
• Exposure to Logging & Monitoring Frameworks  
  – Uses frameworks like SLF4J, Log4j, Logback.  
  – Can integrate basic application performance metrics or tracing for diagnostics (e.g., Micrometer).  

Outcome/Tasks:  
– Creates and configures Spring Boot applications with relevant starters (REST endpoints, data access, etc.).  
– Connects to databases using ORM, applying best practices for data access layer structure and performance.  

Tools:  
– Spring Boot CLI or initializers.  
– Database (PostgreSQL, MySQL) and DB client tools (pgAdmin, MySQL Workbench).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. BUILD, DEPLOYMENT & CONFIGURATION MANAGEMENT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Build Automation  
  – Uses Maven or Gradle effectively (dependency management, multi-module projects, plugin usage).  
  – Understands differences between snapshot and release versions, can manage internal or external dependencies.  
• Environment & Configuration  
  – Employs environment-based profiles, externalized configuration (e.g., application.properties or YAML in Spring).  
  – Manages secrets or sensitive properties (basic usage of vault solutions, environment variables).  
• Integration with CI/CD Pipelines (at a Basic or Intermediate Level)  
  – Commits code to repositories (Git) with relevant branching strategies.  
  – Configures automated builds and tests in Jenkins, GitLab CI, or GitHub Actions.  

Outcome/Tasks:  
– Produces reproducible build artifacts for QA and production environments.  
– Sets up or updates pipeline jobs that compile, test, package, and deploy Java applications.  

Tools:  
– Git for version control (feature branching, code reviews).  
– Jenkins, GitLab CI, or GitHub Actions for continuous integration.  
– Docker for containerizing applications at an elementary level if the organization uses containers.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. TESTING & QUALITY ASSURANCE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Unit & Integration Testing  
  – Designs tests using JUnit, TestNG, or similar frameworks to validate functionality and catch regressions.  
  – Incorporates mocking frameworks (Mockito) for isolating components under test.  
• Test Coverage & Code Quality  
  – Measures test coverage, identifies critical logic paths to ensure coverage is representative.  
  – Understands the importance of integration tests (REST endpoint tests, database access checks).  
• Basic TDD / BDD Exposure  
  – May have experience writing tests first, but does not consistently practice TDD.  
  – Can adapt to BDD frameworks (Cucumber) if required.  

Outcome/Tasks:  
– Ensures code changes are properly validated through automated tests before merging.  
– Works with QA engineers or business analysts to verify application behavior matches requirements.  

Tools:  
– JUnit 5, TestNG, Mockito, AssertJ.  
– Code coverage tools (Jacoco, SonarQube).  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. PERFORMANCE, DEBUGGING & TROUBLESHOOTING
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Diagnostic Skills  
  – Uses logs, debuggers, or basic APM tools (New Relic, Dynatrace) to investigate performance slowdowns.  
  – Interprets thread dumps or heap dumps at a moderate level to pinpoint issues.  
• Performance Optimizations (Intermediate Level)  
  – Identifies suboptimal database queries or excessive memory usage.  
  – Uses profiling tools (VisualVM, YourKit) to find hotspots in CPU or memory usage and propose solutions.  

Outcome/Tasks:  
– Fine-tunes queries or data structures to remove major bottlenecks.  
– Recommends short-term solutions for performance improvements (caching, indexing, concurrency adjustments).  

Tools:  
– VisualVM, JDK Mission Control (JMC), or YourKit for performance analysis.  
– Database performance analysis tools/query profilers.  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8. SECURITY & RELIABILITY AWARENESS
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Basic Security Best Practices  
  – Practices secure coding guidelines: input validation, parameterized queries, secure handling of secrets, HTTPS usage.  
  – Applies standard authentication and authorization practices in frameworks (e.g., Spring Security basics).  
• Resilience & Failover  
  – Has an understanding of how to handle fault tolerance (retries, circuit breakers) but may not have deep experience.  
  – Recognizes the importance of exception handling and graceful degradation.  

Outcome/Tasks:  
– Delivers applications that follow fundamental security standards for data input, data handling, and traffic communication.  
– Ensures that application logs, error handling, and failover logic are not exposing vulnerabilities or private data.  

Tools:  
– Spring Security for basic authentication and authorization.  
– OWASP guidelines for secure coding reference. ...

name: REST APIs
scope: A person with INTERMEDIATE proficiency level in REST APIs as a competency should be able to design, build, document, and consume RESTful APIs following REST principles (statelessness, client-server, cacheability, uniform interface), using proper HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS, HEAD), status codes, and resource-oriented URIs. They can handle request/response structures, content negotiation (JSON, XML), and implement versioning, pagination, filtering, and basic HATEOAS. They use documentation tools like Swagger/OpenAPI, Postman, or API Blueprint, and are familiar with authentication (Basic Auth, API Keys, OAuth 2.0), authorization (RBAC, scopes), and API security best practices (HTTPS, CORS, input validation, rate limiting, protection against injection, CSRF, XSS). They can consume APIs from various clients, integrate with other systems, and understand synchronous/asynchronous calls. They design meaningful error responses, implement input validation (including JSON Schema), and use testing tools like Postman, Insomnia, REST Assured, or JMeter for functional and integration tests. They debug issues using logs, traces, and network tools, optimize performance (latency, caching with headers/ETags), and implement rate limiting/throttling. They are proficient with at least one backend framework (Express.js, Spring Boot, Django REST Framework, Flask, ASP.NET Core), have basic knowledge of API gateways (Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway), and understand monitoring and logging. They are familiar with API lifecycle management (design, deployment, versioning, deprecation), CI/CD pipelines, and can deploy APIs to cloud or on-prem environments. They collaborate effectively with cross-functional teams and communicate API contracts and changes clearly.
long_scope:
Certainly! Here is an exhaustive competency scope for **REST APIs** at the **INTERMEDIATE** proficiency level:

---

## REST APIs – Competency Scope (INTERMEDIATE)

### 1. **Core Concepts & Principles**
- **Understanding of RESTful Architecture:**
  - Solid grasp of REST principles: statelessness, client-server architecture, cacheability, layered system, uniform interface, and code-on-demand (optional).
  - Ability to explain and apply resource-oriented design (nouns, not verbs).
- **HTTP Fundamentals:**
  - Proficient in using HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS, HEAD) appropriately.
  - Clear understanding of idempotency and safety of HTTP methods.
  - Knowledge of HTTP status codes (2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx) and their correct usage in API responses.
- **Resource Modeling:**
  - Ability to design logical and hierarchical resource URIs.
  - Understanding of resource collections, sub-resources, and relationships.
- **Request/Response Handling:**
  - Familiarity with request/response structure, headers, and body.
  - Understanding of content negotiation (Accept, Content-Type headers).
  - Ability to design and consume APIs using JSON and XML payloads.

### 2. **API Design & Documentation**
- **Design Skills:**
  - Ability to design REST APIs that are intuitive, consistent, and maintainable.
  - Familiarity with versioning strategies (URI versioning, header-based, etc.).
  - Understanding of pagination, filtering, and sorting mechanisms.
  - Awareness of HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) and ability to implement basic hypermedia controls.
- **Documentation:**
  - Ability to document APIs using tools such as Swagger/OpenAPI, Postman, or API Blueprint.
  - Understanding of the importance of clear, up-to-date API documentation for consumers.

### 3. **Security**
- **Authentication & Authorization:**
  - Implementation of authentication mechanisms (Basic Auth, API Keys, OAuth 2.0 flows).
  - Understanding of authorization concepts (role-based access control, scopes, permissions).
- **API Security Best Practices:**
  - Knowledge of securing endpoints, input validation, rate limiting, and protection against common attacks (e.g., injection, CSRF, XSS).
  - Familiarity with HTTPS, CORS, and secure transmission of sensitive data.

### 4. **API Consumption & Integration**
- **Client-Side Consumption:**
  - Experience in consuming REST APIs from various clients (web, mobile, backend services) using tools/libraries (e.g., Postman, curl, HTTP clients in programming languages).
- **Integration Patterns:**
  - Ability to integrate REST APIs with other systems and services.
  - Understanding of synchronous vs. asynchronous API calls and their implications.

### 5. **Error Handling & Validation**
- **Error Response Design:**
  - Ability to design and implement meaningful error responses using standard error codes and custom error payloads.
  - Familiarity with error object structures (code, message, details).
- **Input Validation:**
  - Implementation of input validation and sanitization on both client and server sides.
  - Understanding of schema validation (e.g., JSON Schema).

### 6. **Testing & Debugging**
- **API Testing:**
  - Proficiency in writing and executing functional and integration tests for REST APIs.
  - Familiarity with testing tools (Postman, Insomnia, REST Assured, JMeter).
- **Debugging Skills:**
  - Ability to debug API issues using logs, error traces, and network inspection tools.
  - Understanding of common failure scenarios and troubleshooting techniques.

### 7. **Performance & Scalability**
- **Performance Optimization:**
  - Understanding of API performance considerations (latency, throughput).
  - Familiarity with caching strategies (HTTP caching headers, ETags).
- **Rate Limiting & Throttling:**
  - Ability to implement and configure rate limiting and throttling mechanisms.

### 8. **Frameworks, Tools & Technologies**
- **Backend Frameworks:**
  - Proficiency in at least one backend framework for building REST APIs (e.g., Express.js, Spring Boot, Django REST Framework, Flask, ASP.NET Core).
- **API Gateways & Management:**
  - Familiarity with API gateway concepts and basic usage (e.g., Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway).
- **Monitoring & Logging:**
  - Understanding of basic API monitoring and logging practices.
  - Ability to use tools to monitor API health and usage.

### 9. **Deployment & Lifecycle Management**
- **API Lifecycle:**
  - Understanding of API lifecycle stages: design, development, deployment, versioning, deprecation, and retirement.
- **Deployment Practices:**
  - Familiarity with deploying APIs to cloud/on-premise environments.
  - Understanding of CI/CD pipelines for API deployment.

### 10. **Collaboration & Communication**
- **Team Collaboration:**
  - Ability to work with cross-functional teams (frontend, backend, QA, DevOps) in API design and integration.
  - Effective communication of API contracts and changes to stakeholders.

---

**Summary:**  
An INTERMEDIATE professional in REST APIs demonstrates solid proficiency in designing, building, consuming, securing, documenting, testing, and deploying RESTful APIs. They have a strong grasp of REST principles, HTTP fundamentals, and practical implementation skills using modern frameworks and tools. They are capable of handling common integration and security scenarios, optimizing for performance, and collaborating effectively with other teams. However, they may not yet possess deep expertise in advanced topics, large-scale API management, or nuanced architectural trade-offs that distinguish advanced or expert practitioners.

name: ReactJs
scope: An individual with INTERMEDIATE proficiency in React has 3-6 years of experience and a solid grasp of React's core concepts. They can create functional and class components, manage state and props, and understand component lifecycle methods. Familiar with state management libraries like Redux or MobX, they proficiently use hooks—including custom hooks—for better code reusability. They implement routing with React Router, handle forms and validation using libraries like Formik or Yup, and integrate APIs using fetch or Axios. Skilled in styling techniques, they utilize CSS-in-JS libraries and ensure responsive design. They optimize performance through memoization and lazy loading, and write unit tests using Jest and React Testing Library. Familiar with build tools like Webpack and Babel, they can deploy applications to platforms like Netlify or AWS Amplify. They collaborate effectively using Git, participate in code reviews, and are accustomed to Agile methodologies.

name: TypeScript
scope: An intermediate TypeScript developer (3-6 years experience) is proficient in advanced type system features like generics, union and intersection types, type inference and assertions, type guards, and basic mapped and conditional types. They design complex interfaces, implement classes with inheritance, abstract classes, and access modifiers, and organize code using ES6 modules and understand module resolution. They effectively use asynchronous programming with Promises and async/await, handle errors, and write unit and integration tests using frameworks like Jest or Mocha. They configure the TypeScript compiler (tsconfig.json), use build tools like Webpack or Rollup, and enforce code quality with ESLint and Prettier. They develop applications using TypeScript with frameworks like Angular or React, build back-end services with Node.js and TypeScript, and consume RESTful or GraphQL APIs. They participate in system design applying SOLID principles, refactor and optimize code, and implement security best practices. They maintain and improve existing systems, set up CI/CD pipelines, and collaborate using Git and Agile methodologies. They mentor junior developers, contribute to code reviews, document code and APIs, and stay updated with the latest TypeScript features and community developments.

name: PostgreSQL
scope: A person with INTERMEDIATE proficiency level in PostgreSQL as a competency should be able to / is capable of grasping core architecture—postmaster vs. backend processes, shared_buffers, work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, temp_buffers, WAL flow (pg_wal, pg_current_wal_lsn, pg_walfile_name), checkpoints, background writer, autovacuum, MVCC visibility, HOT updates, freezing, hint bits—and exploit views/tools like pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_bgwriter, pg_stat_wal, pg_file_settings and log_line_prefix. They build schemas in 1-5NF with surrogate/natural/composite keys, inheritance, declarative partitioning (RANGE/LIST/HASH, sub-partitions, global/local indexes), tablespaces, domains, enums, collations, JSONB, arrays and range types, documenting via ERDs and versioning with Liquibase, Flyway or Sqitch. They craft SQL using CTEs (materialised and inline), window functions, set ops, LATERAL, FILTER aggregates, INSERT … ON CONFLICT, generated/identity columns, COPY, and FDWs (postgres_fdw, file_fdw, mysql_fdw, jdbc_fdw) while leaning on psql, pgAdmin, DBeaver, pgFormatter and pgsql-lint. They write PL/pgSQL with exceptions, security DEFINER/INVOKER, statement-/row-level triggers, transition tables, LISTEN/NOTIFY, basic logical decoding via pgoutput, debug with pldbgapi and auto_explain, and extend with plpython3u. They design B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, hash, expression, partial and covering indexes, decode EXPLAIN ANALYZE BUFFERS VERBOSE, understand bitmap vs. index-only scans, page splits, visibility map and bloat, and maintain with VACUUM (INDEX_CLEANUP), autovacuum tuning, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, pg_stat_statements and pg_waldump. They handle transactions and concurrency—ACID snapshots, READ COMMITTED/REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE, advisory locks, SKIP LOCKED, NOWAIT—resolve deadlocks via pg_locks and blocking_pids, and use pg_cancel_backend or pg_terminate_backend safely. They tune performance by adjusting shared_buffers, effective_cache_size, work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, max_parallel_workers_per_gather, wal_compression, planner cost constants and enable_* flags, leverage parallel query, pg_stat_all_tables, pg_stat_io, pg_stat_kcache, pgbench, pgBadger, pg_stat_monitor, auto_explain, iostat, vmstat and perf, plus optimise I/O layout, FILLFACTOR and autovacuum_freeze_max_age. They secure dependable backups with pg_dump/pg_dumpall, pg_basebackup, compression/encryption, WAL archiving, restore_command, recovery_target_time, PITR, pg_amcheck, CHECKPOINT control, schedule via cron/pg_cron, and use pgBackRest, Barman, WAL-G, pg_repack and pg_partman. They deploy streaming replication with synchronous_commit, physical/logical slots, analyse lag, manage hot_standby_feedback and max_standby_streaming_delay, run pg_basebackup --write-recovery-conf and pg_ctl promote, orchestrate failovers with repmgr, Patroni or pg_auto_failover, and prototype logical flows with pg_logical or test_decoding. They enforce security through role hierarchies, hardened search_path, row-level security, SSL/TLS, client-cert, SCRAM-SHA-256, pg_hba.conf, logging_collector, log_statement, pgaudit and pgcrypto. They evaluate and manage extensions (uuid-ossp, hstore, citext, pg_trgm, PostGIS, auth_delay, pg_stat_statements), integrate with Hibernate, SQLAlchemy, Django ORM via PgBouncer (transaction/session), package with Docker official images, CrunchyData/Zalando operators, Ansible, Helm, Terraform, monitor in Prometheus + Grafana, run CI/CD migrations with Git, feature flags and shadow tables, and handle incidents through PagerDuty or OpsGenie.
long_scope:
INTERMEDIATE-LEVEL POSTGRESQL – COMPETENCY SCOPE (≈ 3-5 years hands-on experience)

General profile  
• Delivers medium-complexity database solutions with moderate supervision.  
• Owns day-to-day operation of one or more production clusters; escalates only atypical or deep-internals issues.  
• Collaborates effectively with application engineers, DevOps/SRE and data analysts, translating functional requirements into performant relational designs.  
• Comfortable coaching juniors on fundamentals; still looks to senior staff for architectural or edge-case guidance.

The scope below is organised as outcome-oriented capability groups.  Each group states what the professional must be able to accomplish, what knowledge underpins it, what artefacts or deliverables result, and what tools or subsystems are normally employed.  Coverage is intentionally exhaustive for the INTERMEDIATE band.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Foundation & Architecture Awareness
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Chooses configuration and operational tactics that align with PostgreSQL’s execution model and storage architecture.  
• Anticipates how design or code changes propagate to WAL, shared buffers, background writer, check-pointer, autovacuum and logical/physical replication workers.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• Postmaster vs. backend processes; memory contexts (shared buffers, work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, temp_buffers).  
• Checkpoint & WAL write sequence, recycle/archival flow.  
• Conceptual file layout (base/…/relfilenode, pg_wal, pg_tblspc, pg_multixact, pg_commit_ts).  
• MVCC visibility timeline; HOT updates, tuple freezing threshold, hint bits.

TOOLS & SUBSYSTEMS  
• system catalog introspection (pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_bgwriter, pg_stat_wal, pg_file_settings).  
• log_line_prefix tuning, csvlog, pg_current_wal_lsn(), pg_walfile_name().

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Relational & Physical Data Modelling
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Produces schemas that balance normalisation, denormalisation and partitioning for performance, maintainability and storage cost.  
• Selects optimal built-in types (including JSONB, arrays, rangetypes) or domain types to enforce business rules.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• Normal forms 1-5, surrogate vs. natural keys, composite keys, inheritance vs. partitioning.  
• Declarative partitioning (RANGE, LIST, HASH); criteria for sub-partitioning; global vs. local indexes.  
• Collation handling, enum evolution strategies, character encoding implications.

ARTIFACTS  
• Entity–Relation diagrams, DDL migration scripts, versioned schema repositories (Liquibase / Flyway / Sqitch).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Core SQL Proficiency
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Writes clear, set-oriented SQL that uses the planner efficiently; refactors procedural logic to SQL-native constructs where possible.  
• Produces deterministic DDL/DML respecting transactional semantics.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• SELECT pipeline, CTEs (non-materialised vs. materialised), window functions, set operations, lateral joins, variadic aggregates, FILTER clause.  
• INSERT … ON CONFLICT, generated columns, identity columns vs. serial.  
• Data type casts, search_path behaviour, collations, role-dependent default settings.  
• COPY / \copy for bulk ingest; FOREIGN DATA WRAPPER landscape (postgres_fdw, file_fdw, mysql_fdw, jdbc_fdw) for federation tasks.

TOOLS  
• psql advanced features (\gexec, \watch, pset), pgAdmin / DBeaver for visual work, code linters (pgFormatter, pgsql-lint).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Procedural & Reactive Programming
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Packages business logic that truly belongs in the database while avoiding over-use of procedural code.  
• Implements data-driven side effects (triggers, NOTIFY/LISTEN) with predictable performance.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• PL/pgSQL control structures, exception blocks, security definer vs. invoker, variable scope, STRICT vs. RETURNS NULL ON NULL.  
• Row-level vs. statement-level triggers, transition tables, trigger execution order.  
• Event mechanisms: LISTEN/NOTIFY payload size limits, logical decoding basics, pgoutput plugin concept.

TOOLS  
• psql debugger (edb-psql, pldbgapi), auto_explain for PL blocks, extension management (CREATE EXTENSION plpython3u).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. Indexing Strategy & Data Access Paths
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Designs, measures and maintains index structures that satisfy query patterns with minimal write overhead.  
• Reads EXPLAIN output fluently, correlating plan nodes to index characteristics.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• B-tree mechanics (clustering, fillfactor, page splits), GIN, GiST, BRIN, hash indices; expression, partial and covering indexes.  
• Bitmap vs. index-only scans, visibility map, HOT/pruning impact.  
• Maintenance routines: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM (INDEX_CLEANUP), autovacuum thresholds tuning.

TOOLS  
• EXPLAIN (ANALYZE BUFFERS VERBOSE), pg_stat_statements, auto_explain, pg_waldump for bloat analysis.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Transactionality & Concurrency Control
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Builds application flows that exploit PostgreSQL’s MVCC without unnecessary locks or race conditions.  
• Investigates and resolves deadlocks, long-running transactions and vacuum freeze issues.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• ACID guarantees, snapshot semantics, pg_locks view, lock escalation path.  
• Isolation levels (READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE) with use-case guidance.  
• Advisory locks, SKIP LOCKED / NOWAIT qualifiers.

TOOLS  
• blocking_pids query patterns, pg_stat_activity states, pg_stat_progress_vacuum, pg_terminate_backend() vs. pg_cancel_backend().

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Performance Diagnostics & Tuning
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Conducts systematic performance investigations: formulate hypothesis, collect evidence, test improvements, document outcomes.  
• Adjusts GUCs and schema objects for steady-state performance in clusters up to hundreds of GBs and thousands of TPS.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• Resource management parameters (shared_buffers, work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, effective_cache_size, max_parallel_workers_per_gather, wal_compression).  
• Planner cost constants, enable_* toggles, parallel query eligibility.  
• I/O layout: tablespaces, FILLFACTOR, autovacuum_freeze_max_age.

TOOLS  
• pg_stat_all_tables/indexes, pg_stat_io (16+), pg_stat_kcache, pgbench, pgBadger, pg_stat_monitor; OS-level tools (iostat, vmstat, perf).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
8. Maintenance, Backup & Recovery
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Guarantees RPO/RTO that match business SLAs through appropriate backup topologies and periodic recovery drills.  
• Schedules and validates maintenance tasks without significant production impact.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• Logical vs. physical backup (pg_dump[all] vs. pg_basebackup), custom format, directory format, compression/encryption options.  
• WAL archiving, restore_command / recovery_target_time, point-in-time recovery workflow.  
• VACUUM variants, ANALYZE statistics targets, pg_amcheck, CHECKPOINT interactions.

TOOLS  
• cron/pg_cron, pgBackRest, Barman, WAL-G, pg_repack, pg_partman; shell scripting with psql \COPY for seed data.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
9. Replication & High Availability (Foundational)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Deploys and administers primary-standby architectures, executes planned failover/switchover, investigates replication lag.  
• Implements basic logical replication for selective table migration or blue-green rollout.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• Streaming replication lifecycle, synchronous_commit modes, slot types (physical vs. logical), slot lag measurement.  
• Replication conflicts and resolution (hot_standby_feedback, max_standby_streaming_delay).  
• Failover orchestration patterns (repmgr, Patroni, pg_auto_failover) – not deep internals, but operational familiarity.

TOOLS  
• pg_basebackup --write-recovery-conf, pg_ctl promote, repmgr client, patronictl, pg_logical, test_decoding.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
10. Security & Compliance Controls
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Implements least-privilege role hierarchies, credential rotation and connection encryption.  
• Supports application audits by producing reliable logs and row-level history where required.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• Role attributes, membership inheritance, SECURE SEARCH_PATH usage, row-level security policies.  
• SSL/TLS setup, client-cert auth, SCRAM-SHA-256 lifecycle; pg_hba.conf rules evaluation order.  
• Logging_collector, log_statement, pgaudit extension basics, column-level encryption patterns (pgcrypto, client-side libs).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
11. Extension & Ecosystem Competence
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Evaluates, installs and maintains common extensions while weighing version compatibility and supportability.  
• Integrates PostgreSQL with ORMs, ETL and BI stacks, handling type mapping and performance tuning issues.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• Extension packaging versus contrib, CREATE EXTENSION privilege, control files, ALTER EXTENSION UPDATE.  
• Core ecosystem: uuid-ossp, hstore, citext, pg_trgm, PostGIS (user-level use, not deep GIS), auth_delay, pg_stat_statements.  
• ORMs (Hibernate, SQLAlchemy, Django ORM) dialect peculiarities, connection-pooling layers (PgBouncer transaction vs. session pooling).

TOOLS  
• ALTER EXTENSION, shared_preload_libraries management, Docker Official PostgreSQL images, Kubernetes operators (CrunchyData / Zalando).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
12. Collaboration, Documentation & Process Integration
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OUTCOMES  
• Embeds database deliverables into CI/CD pipelines, peer-reviews SQL/DDL in merge requests, documents operational runbooks.  
• Translates monitoring data into actionable dashboard and incident response playbooks.

KNOWLEDGE COMPONENTS  
• Declarative infrastructure (Ansible roles, Helm charts, Terraform modules) for PostgreSQL artifacts.  
• Migration gating strategies (feature flags, shadow tables, backfill jobs).  
• SLA/SLO definition, on-call handover protocols.

TOOLS  
• Git, Liquibase/Flyway checks, Prometheus + Grafana dashboards, Incident-response platforms (PagerDuty, OpsGenie).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Boundaries of INTERMEDIATE Level
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
• Does NOT yet engineer custom C extensions, custom access methods or deep planner hacking.  
• Seeks guidance for advanced multi-region replication, sharding, write-scaling topologies, or zero-downtime major-version upgrades.  
• Recognises on-disk corruption signatures but escalates root-cause analysis to advanced/experts.  
• Reads, but seldom modifies, PostgreSQL source code.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Someone operating comfortably across the twelve capability groups above—with minimal supervision and with demonstrable, repeatable outcomes—meets the definition of INTERMEDIATE proficiency in PostgreSQL for the purposes of interview question design.
